title: Respective roles of remote and local wind stress forcings in the development of warm SST errors in the South-Eastern Tropical Atlantic in a coupled high-resolution model
problem: Coupled climate models exhibit a persistent warm sea surface temperature bias in the South-Eastern Tropical Atlantic, but the relative contributions of remote equatorial wind errors and local atmospheric and oceanic processes to this bias are not well understood.
method: This study performs seasonal hindcasts and sensitivity experiments, replacing modeled wind stress with observations in key regions, to diagnose the respective roles of remote and local forcings in the development of warm sea surface temperature bias in the South-Eastern Tropical Atlantic.
task: The task is to determine the respective roles of remote equatorial and local wind stress forcings in the development of warm sea surface temperature errors in the South-Eastern Tropical Atlantic using a high-resolution coupled climate model and sensitivity experiments.
innovation: This paper uses a high-resolution climate model to demonstrate that the warm SST bias in the South-Eastern Tropical Atlantic is primarily driven by remote equatorial westerly wind errors, which explain about 57% of the bias in March-May through anomalous warm horizontal advection.

Both versions of the model use the same land surface scheme ISBA. However, in the LR version ISBA is externalized through the use of the SURFface Externalisée (SURFEX) modeling platform developed at Météo-France.

Other minor (relative to the focus of the present study) differences between the HR and LR models consist in using of different sea-ice models (GELATO v5 (Salas-Mélia 2002) for the LR version) and in using a river routing model [TRIP, Oki and Sud (1998)] in the LR version in contrast to the HR version that uses a climatological river transport to the ocean.

Processes involved in the development of the warm sea surface temperature (SST) bias in the Tropical South-Eastern Atlantic (SETA) in a high resolution (HR) version of the CNRM-CM model are evaluated based on full-field initialized seasonal hindcasts starting at 1 February of each year for 2000–2009.

The intensity of the wind-driven coastal upwelling in the SETA is dynamically linked to the strength of the equatorward Benguela current. The Benguela current causes equatorward advection of cool water along the coast from the southern tip of Africa to about 16°S, where it meets the warm southward-flowing Angola Current (e.g. Shannon et al. 1987).

Previous studies (Richter et al. 2012; Xu et al. 2014b) suggested that the mechanism for the formation of the warm SETA biases in climate models resembled that of the development of interannual warm events that are induced by a relaxation of equatorial trade winds and that manifest themselves as a Benguela Niño in March-April-May (MAM), followed by an Atlantic Niño in the eastern equatorial region in June-July (Lübbecke et al. 2010; Imbol Kougue et al. 2017).

Two main mechanisms are used in literature to explain this oceanic teleconnection: mean horizontal advection and Kelvin waves propagating along the equator and then along the western coast of southern Africa (e.g. Xu et al. 2014b).
